summary: Presents Internet Architecture Board concerns that continuing research is needed to evolve the Internet infrastructure, and that steady, non-commercial funding is needed to support it. It is an opinion statement rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A group that looks after the internet says that explorers need support to keep it growing, and they need steady funding that is not tied to a company.

why internet research needs non-commercial funding

subtitle: A call for sustained, non-commercial funding to evolve the Internet.

tldr.problem: Internet infrastructure research needs steady funding, but commercial funding focuses on short-term competitive advantage and basic research is underfunded. Without non-commercial funding, critical Internet evolution may stall.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board documents the history of Internet research funding and identifies open research areas (naming, routing, security, measurement) that merit continued investment and are unlikely to be funded by industry alone.
tldr.outcome: The document makes a case for governments and non-commercial sponsors to fund Internet research consistently, demonstrating the breadth of unsolved problems and the historical importance of non-commercial funding.

today: RFC 3869 is an Informational RFC expressing the IAB's policy views on research funding. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the board's statement on the topic.

sections.title: The Funding Challenge and Historical Context
sections.content:
This RFC is an opinion statement from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), not a technical specification. The IAB observes that Internet infrastructure research faces a funding crisis. In the 1980s and early 1990s, the U.S. government (through DARPA and NSF) funded basic research that led to the web, email protocols, and routing algorithms. Starting in the mid-1990s, governments stepped back, assuming commercial firms would fund whatever was needed.

In practice, commercial funding has focused on products and competitive advantage, not foundational research. Higher-risk innovations and work on shared infrastructure rarely get funded by industry because no single company owns or benefits from global Internet improvements. The result is a decline in research on core Internet evolution.
sections.plainLanguage: Long ago, governments paid people to invent the internet and email. Later, companies took over, but companies only pay for things that make them money. Now important research isn't getting done because nobody's funding it.

sections.title: The Breadth of Open Research Questions
sections.content:
The IAB identifies major research areas where progress is needed but unlikely to come from commercial funding alone. In naming and DNS, the system works well but has scaling challenges; research into caching, security (DNSSEC), and alternative transport protocols is needed. In routing, the system handles 150,000 to 200,000 prefixes but may hit algorithmic limits before 300,000; research is needed into convergence times, multi-homing, and next-generation architectures. Routing integrity and authentication present unsolved problems without clear commercial payoff.

Security research spans cryptography, key management, denial-of-service defense, and deployment practices. Network management needs work on autonomous systems, enhanced monitoring, and customer-facing tools. Mobile and ad-hoc routing are emerging areas without mature solutions. Measurement and modeling of the Internet's behavior is fundamental but lacks funding.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet has lots of unsolved problems: what if too many addresses get added to routing tables? How do we keep DNS fast? How do we make mobile networks work? Scientists need time and money to figure these out.

sections.title: The Role of Non-Commercial Funding in Internet Evolution
sections.content:
The RFC traces how Internet research funding has shaped what exists. In the 1970s and 1980s, DARPA funded three different network types (ARPAnet, packet radio, packet satellite). The need to connect them drove the invention of IP and internetworking. This research had no commercial payoff at the time but was essential.

In the 1980s, NSF funded academic networking, which created infrastructure that students used and later commercialized. NSF's investment in supercomputing networks indirectly created the environment where the Web was invented. The document argues that this history shows non-commercial research funding creates the foundation for later commercial success.
sections.plainLanguage: The government funded early internet research even though there was no money to be made. Those government investments led to the things companies now profit from. We need to do that again.

sections.title: Why Commercial Funding Is Insufficient
sections.content:
The IAB notes that while commercial funding has enabled transition of research into products, it systematically under-funds research that doesn't offer short-term competitive advantage. No single company owns global Internet infrastructure, so research to improve it collectively benefits all competitors equally. This free-rider problem means companies rationally avoid funding it. Additionally, commercial funding tends toward vocationally-focused education and equipment donations rather than fundamental research.

Startup companies, which historically commercialize cutting-edge research, cannot themselves afford to fund research. Established firms are good at buying startups but not at advancing the fundamental research that startups depend on. For areas like routing architecture, measurement infrastructure, and security fundamentals, there is simply no market mechanism to drive research forward.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies like paying for things that make them money faster than competitors. But research that helps everyone doesn't help any one company more than others. So it doesn't get funded. And small startups that might do research can't afford to pay researchers.

sections.title: The Call for Sustained Non-Commercial Research Support
sections.content:
The IAB's central recommendation is that governments and non-commercial organizations should increase and sustain funding for both basic and applied Internet research. The RFC emphasizes that it is not prescriptive about which specific projects should be funded; rather, it presents evidence that ongoing research is needed across many domains and that commercial funding alone cannot meet the need.

The document notes that research includes not just theory but also implementation, deployment, and evaluation. It calls for support for freely distributable prototypes, test-beds, and measurement infrastructure that the entire research community can use. The implicit model is the historical one: government funding creates shared research infrastructure and foundations that the commercial sector later builds upon.
sections.plainLanguage: Governments should fund internet research the way they used to. Give money to researchers to study hard problems, build working examples, and share what they learn with everyone. Companies will build on that later.
